In January 2015, Stephen Hawking along with Elon Musk and many Al
experts, signed an open letter on artificial intelligence,
calling for serious research into its impact on society. In the past, Elon
Musk has warned that superhuman artificial intelligence is
capable of providing incalculable benefits, but if deployed incautiously, will
have an adverse effect on the human race. He and I
sit on the scientific advisory board for Future of Life Institute, an
organisation working to mitigate existential risk facing
humanity. This called for concrete research on how we could prevent
potential problems while also reaping the potential
benefits Al offers us, and is designed to get Al researchers and developers
to pay more attention to Al safety.
 
Recent developments in the advancement of Al include a call by the
European Parliament for drafting a set of regulations to
govern the creation of robots and Al. A report presented to the Parliament
declares that the world is on the cusp of a new
industrial robot revolution. It stresses that at all times researchers and
designers should ensure all robotic design incorporates a
kill switch. There is a possibility that within a few decades Al could surpass
human intellectual capacity and challenge the
human-robot relationship.
 
By 2025, there will be about 30 mega cities with more than 10 million
inhabitants. Robots will definitely speed up the retail
process, but to revolutionise shopping, they need to be fast enough to
allow same-day delivery on every order. Recent Al
landmarks such as self-driving cars, or a computer game winning at the
game of Go, etc. are signs of what is to come. Enormous
levels of investment are pouring into this technology which will eventually
permeate every aspect of society including health
care, work, education and science.
 
Our future is a race between the growing power of a technology and the
wisdom with which we use it!

ensure that all robotic design incorporates a kill switch because :

Tirunelveli district in Madras state. He was an

teaching of the Vedas and the ideas of Vedantic Humanism. Bharati was in

questionText:
Read the given passage and answer the questions that follow :-
 
Words have their limitations and those who write, or those who read, also
have their limitations or their own frameworks to
understand words. Many words start their journey with some meaning, but
over the centuries they gather different nuances or
acquire a totally different meaning. When the writer uses a specific word
with some specific meaning in mind, it is not necessary
that the reader will have exactly the same meaning in mind while reading.
Thus, the communication, and the intent of the writer
gets hampered. The problem increases manifold when we talk about
essentially Indian concepts in English.
 
Several Sanskrit words like Dharma, Yajna, Srishti, Jeevan Darshan,
Ishvara, and Aatman are untranslatable in English, as of
course, there are words in English like 'religion', 'secularism', 'exclusivism',

'theology', 'ideology', etc. which are untranslatable in
Indian languages. These are not just words. They denote the characteristic
thought process of that culture, which the people
belonging to that culture can understand in that one word, but others
outside that culture would need long explanation and yet
may not grasp its meaning. Generally, people try to understand the word in
the context of their cultural experience.
 
Thus, 'religion' is understood as Dharma by many Indians, whereas it is not
Dharma. Dharma is understood as 'religion' by
West-oriented thinkers, Indians and non-Indians. Similarly, Secularism is
understood as equal treatment of all religions in India,
whereas that is not its meaning in Europe. The usage of terms and their
inherent meanings is a big topic in itself.
Which of the following statements is true according to the given passage ?
 
(A) A word is absolutely free from its usage and cultural influences.
(B) The reader interprets what the writer means by admiring the
qualifications of the writer.
(C) The act of reading is free from personal biases and opinions.
(D) A word gathers different meanings over time, context and place.
 
Choose the correct answer from the options given below :-

I still remember the summers of my childhood, when the air in our
ancestral village carried the scent of ripening mangoes. Our orchard, an
expanse of towering trees with branches heavy with fruit, was my
sanctuary. The afternoons were spent sprawled on a charpoy under the
largest tree, listening to my grandmother's tales of kings and sages, while
the cicadas hummed a lazy tune.
 
One evening, when the sky blushed orange, my cousin Rohan and I dared
each other to climb the ancient mango tree—the one no one had scaled in
years. "It's cursed," the elders warned, "a snake guards its highest
branches." But we were twelve, and fear was something we laughed at.
With scraped knees and racing hearts, we ascended, our fingers sticky
with the sweetness of half-eaten mangoes.
 
Then, suddenly, I froze. Just inches from my hand, nestled between two
branches, lay a coiled serpent, its beady eyes fixed upon me. Panic gripped
my chest, my breath shallow. "Don't move," Rohan whispered. Trembling, I
heeded his words, inching backward ever so slowly. As soon as my feet hit
the ground, I bolted, my heart pounding louder than the temple bells at
dusk.
 
We never climbed that tree again. But to this day, whenever I taste a
mango, I remember that evening—the thrill, the terror, and the inexplicable
joy of childhood.

questionText:
Read the passage given below and answer the four questions that follow :-
 
Earlier this year, my daughter moved into college, where I noticed her
neighbour's vision board filled with quotes and photos of
physicians. The neighbour's mother explained it was meant to inspire her
daughter, aspiring to be a pediatrician, to "manifest"
her goal. Manifestation, popularized by The Secret, suggests desires can
become reality through focused thought. Neuro-
scientists James Doty and Sabina Brennan explore how brain function
supports this idea, offering practical approaches to
achieving goals.
 
Doty's Mind Magic dismisses magical thinking, emphasizing a scientific
approach to cultivating resilience and focus. His six-week
plan teaches readers to embed intentions into their subconscious, rewire
brain networks, and improve attention to
opportunities. He argues that manifesting clarifies desires and aligns
thoughts with purposeful action, transforming goals into
reality.
 
Brennan's The Neuroscience of Manifesting also debunks myths around
manifestation, explaining how intentional thinking shifts
perception and behaviour. She highlights the brain's negativity bias and
advocates redirecting attention to positive, goal-
oriented thoughts. Brennan introduces the "seven Cs of manifesting"-
curiosity, compassion, connection, change, clarity,
coherence, and creation - drawing from neuroscience and psychology to
explain how intentional focus can lead to success.
 
Both authors argue that tools like vision boards are not about magical
outcomes but rather activating brain networks like the
reticular activation system to reinforce goals. By stimulating focus and
motivation, such tools help translate aspirations into
action. Ultimately, Doty and Brennan remind us that achieving our
ambitions depends on intention, focus, and actionable
change -a "real magic" rooted in our own brains and behaviours.
What is the main purpose of tools like vision boards, according to the text?

options.text: To communicate desires to the universe
options.mistakeAnalysis: Incorrect option. Inverts the governing property or boundary condition.

options.text: To enhance creativity and artistic skills
options.mistakeAnalysis: Incorrect option. Applies an adjacent or reciprocal mathematical relation.

options.text: To visually remind individuals of their goals
options.mistakeAnalysis: Correct answer. Accurately solves the problem for Inference and Main Idea.

options.text: To provide a shortcut to achieving success
options.mistakeAnalysis: Incorrect option. Confuses related NCERT concepts or attributes.

detailedSolution:
Detailed Solution:
For Inference and Main Idea (Reading Comprehension):
Step 1: Identify the specific reference to 'vision boards' in the text. The last paragraph states: 'Both authors argue that tools like vision boards are not about magical outcomes but rather activating brain networks like the reticular activation system to reinforce goals.' Step 2: Analyze the function described. The text says they 'reinforce goals' and 'stimulate focus and motivation'. Step 3: Evaluate Option A ('communicate desires to the universe'). The text explicitly dismisses 'magical thinking' and 'magical outcomes', so this is incorrect. Step 4: Evaluate Option B ('visually remind individuals of their goals'). This aligns with 'reinforcing goals' and 'stimulating focus' by keeping the goal in mind (visual reminder), which activates the brain's attention mechanisms. Step 5: Evaluate Option C ('enhance creativity and artistic skills'). The text mentions 'creation' as one of the 7 Cs, but the primary purpose of the board itself is goal reinforcement, not artistic skill development. Step 6: Evaluate Option D ('provide a shortcut to achieving success'). The text emphasizes 'actionable change', 'focus', and 'intention', implying effort and process, not a shortcut.

Therefore, option (C) is the correct answer.

Unless one is wealthy, there is no use in being a charming fellow. Romance
is the privilege of the rich, not the profession of the
unemployed. The poor should be practical and prosaic. It is better to have
a permanent income than to be fascinating. These are
the great truths of modern life which Hughie Erskine never realized.
Intellectually, he was not of much importance. He never said
a brilliant or even ill-natured thing in his life. But he was wonderfully good-
looking, as popular with men as he was with women,
and had every accomplishment except making money. His father had
bequeathed him a cavalry sword and a History of the
Peninsular War in fifteen volumes. Hughie hung the first over his looking-
glass, put the second on a shelf between Ruff's Guide
and Bailey's Magazine, and lived on two hundred a year from an old aunt.
He had tried everything. He had gone on the Stock
Exchange for six months; but what was a butterfly to do among bulls and
bears? He had been a tea-merchant for a little longer
but soon tired of pekoe and souchong. Then he tried selling dry sherry.
That did not answer. Ultimately, he became nothing; a
delightful, ineffectual young man with a perfect profile and no profession.
 
To make matters worse, he was in love with Laura Merton, the daughter of
a retired Colonel. Laura adored him, and he
worshipped her, but neither had a penny to their name. Though the Colonel
liked Hughie, he refused to approve their
engagement.

Every time a child takes a soft drink, is he laying the ground­work for a
dangerous bone disease? Fizzy and sugary drinks don’t cause
osteoporosis but, because they are often a substitute for a glass of milk,
children miss out on taking in the calcium and vitamin D they need to build
a strong skeleton. Many of them also lead a sedentary lifestyle, so they

children tend to suffer from brittle bones and frac­tures later on in life. In

women in India, it also menaces over 12 million men.
